# Outcomes analysis — §14.4

*Generated by `src/outcomes_analysis.py`. Out-of-time test window, scored once.*

## 1. The backtest

| | |
|---|---:|
| test rows | 4,340 |
| realised distress events | 985 |
| operating threshold (§8.4, chosen on validation) | 0.245 |
| **false negatives** | **24** |
| recall at threshold | 97.6% |

## 2. Every false negative, reviewed

§14.4 asks one question of each miss: *was the signal present in the data but
unused, or genuinely absent?* The answer is decided against the **training
window's** own distribution, never the test window's — letting the outcome
define what counts as a warning sign would be circular.

For each of the 11 features whose tail carries at least
1.25x the base distress rate in training, the adverse direction and its
20% cut are recorded in `adverse_profile.json`. A miss is then:

| verdict | n | meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| SIGNAL ABSENT | 12 | nothing available was in a historically adverse tail — a limit of the data |
| SIGNAL UNUSED | 11 | something was, and the model scored through it — a limit of the model |
| DATA MISSING | 1 | over half the features null; the firm was unscoreable in substance |

`DATA MISSING` is kept separate deliberately. Folding it into `SIGNAL ABSENT`
would credit the data with an absence it never had the chance to demonstrate,
and would quietly convert the model's refusal to guess into the model being
wrong.

## 3. Calibration by decile

Ranking can be excellent while the probability is not a probability, and the
§8.4 cost-optimal threshold is applied to the **probability**, not to the rank.
A systematic gap here would mean the threshold is cutting at a different real
risk level than it claims to.

| decile | n | predicted | observed | gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 434 | 0.0008 | 0 | -0.0008 |
| 2 | 434 | 0.0017 | 0 | -0.0017 |
| 3 | 434 | 0.0035 | 0 | -0.0035 |
| 4 | 434 | 0.0074 | 0.0023 | -0.0051 |
| 5 | 434 | 0.0207 | 0.0046 | -0.0161 |
| 6 | 434 | 0.1053 | 0.0346 | -0.0708 |
| 7 | 434 | 0.3775 | 0.2166 | -0.1609 |
| 8 | 434 | 0.698 | 0.4516 | -0.2464 |
| 9 | 434 | 0.8787 | 0.6613 | -0.2174 |
| 10 | 434 | 0.9732 | 0.8986 | -0.0746 |

`gap` is observed minus predicted; positive means the model is under-confident
in that decile.

**The model is systematically OVER-confident in the upper deciles, and this must be stated wherever a probability is shown.** Mean gap across deciles 7-10 is -0.175; the worst is decile 8, which predicts 69.8% against a realised 45.2%.

The cause is not a defect but a choice: `scale_pos_weight` is applied on the training window to handle imbalance (§8.4), and re-weighting the positive class inflates predicted probabilities by construction. **Ranking is unaffected** — AUC, KS and the ordering the product actually uses are all rank statistics, and the operating threshold was chosen on validation under the same distortion, so the flag/no-flag decision is sound.

What is *not* sound is reading the number as a probability. A firm shown at 70% has a realised rate nearer 45%. Either the dashboard presents the score as a risk *rank* rather than a likelihood, or a calibration layer (Platt or isotonic, fitted on the validation window only) is fitted before the number is shown. The first is cheaper and is what §12.3's risk bands already do; the second is the right fix if a probability is ever quoted to a user.

## 4. What this does not do

This is a backtest on a held-out window, not a production outcomes loop. The
test window is the most recent data in the panel, so there is no later cohort
to score and then wait on. A real §14.4 loop runs annually as each fiscal
year's outcomes resolve; this is the first iteration of it, and the harness it
will run in.
